one_liner: Header-only inline memcpy/memset/memmove from the freestanding micron libc/STL rewrite; 1.13-1.91x fewer cycles than glibc on SPEC2017-size random copies.
what_it_does: micron is a single-author, header-only C++23 reimplementation of libc and the C++ standard library that talks to Linux syscalls directly; its memory/cmemory headers provide mc::memcpy, mc::memmove, mc::memset, memcmp and memchr. The mc:: functions are templates over typed pointers, not the C signature: memcpy and memmove take an element count, memset a byte count. C-ABI memcpy/memmove/memset symbols are emitted only in freestanding builds (duck -k), so in a normal hosted program you call mc::memcpy explicitly rather than replacing ::memcpy.
how_it_is_fast: Copies up to 256 bytes (128 without AVX2) go through an always_inline size ladder that loads the head and tail with overlapping 2/4/8/16/32-byte moves and issues all loads before any store, the same unaligned head/tail technique glibc's memmove-vec-unaligned-erms uses, so memmove shares the code. Larger sizes go to a noinline tier chosen from a one-time CPUID probe: a vector loop below the rep threshold, rep movsb from 2112 bytes (FSRM) or 8192 bytes (ERMS), and non-temporal stores above max(L3/4, 1 MiB). Because the ladder is inlined into the caller, small variable-size copies avoid the out-of-line call, PLT jump and ifunc-selected entry that ::memcpy pays.
when_to_use: Projects already built on micron, or freestanding/no-libc Linux binaries that need fast mem* routines without glibc.

Hot loops issuing many small variable-size copies (the SPEC2017 mix: mean 104 bytes, 77% of calls at 32 bytes or less) over working sets of 32 KiB to 1 MiB, where inlining the size ladder removes per-call overhead.
Zero-filling buffers in cache-resident working sets: memset of zero won 1.13x at 32 KiB to 1.91x at 1 MiB in the random-size run and 222 of 386 hot cells in the detail run.
x86-64 Linux builds with -march=native on AVX2-class cores (results come from a Haswell-E i7-5960X).
when_not_to_use: Cold-cache or streaming copies: glibc won all 14 cold memcpy cells (geomean libc/micron 0.85) and 11 of 14 cold memset cells in the author's detail file.
Tiny memmoves and non-zero memset: glibc took 3-byte memmove at 0.27 vs 1.12 cycles/byte and won 29 of 50 hot memset cells with fill byte 0x5A.
Hosted programs wanting a global ::memcpy replacement: the C-ABI symbols exist only in freestanding builds, and the mc:: API has different semantics.

Non-Linux targets or code that needs a stable ABI: Linux is the only supported OS, aarch64 and i386 are 'compiles, untested', and the README says the ABI may change without notice and that performance takes precedence over safety.
Teams needing an independently reviewed routine: 13 stars, one author, no external measurements, and evidence only from a single Haswell-E machine with an unstated glibc version.

integration.dependencies: none outside the repo, but cmemory pulls micron's types, type_traits, attributes and simd headers; hosted builds link glibc/pthread by default
integration.min_toolchain: C++23 (GCC or Clang through duck's flag profiles; the benchmark files cite GCC 16.2.1; duck itself is bootstrapped with -std=c++26)
integration.platforms: Linux only; x86-64 (SSE2 floor, AVX2 and AVX-512 tiers via -march), armv7-a; aarch64 and i386 compile but are untested
integration.thread_safety: Routines are stateless; the one-time CPUID tunables probe is guarded by an atomic compare-and-swap in __mem_tun_get (hosted) or run from _start (freestanding).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: mc::memcpy/mc::memmove take typed pointers and an element count, mc::memset a byte count; C-ABI memcpy/memmove/memset replacements are generated only in freestanding (-k) builds

gotchas: Harness asymmetry behind the numbers: benches/memory_random_bench.cpp inlines mc::memcpy/memset/memmove into the timed loop, while ::memcpy is an out-of-line glibc call through the PLT. At 32 KiB the memcpy gap is about 7 cycles per call (0.0677 cycles/byte x 104-byte mean size, derived from page data), roughly the cost of that call, so part of the 1.24-1.59x reflects call elimination rather than a faster copy loop. memset_rand fills only zero, the one fill value where micron wins in its own detail file.

The random benchmark never compares micron's output with libc's. The repo's tests/memory/mem_exhaustive_small.cpp (0-300 bytes at every offset, with sentinel guards) and mem_overlap_exhaustive.cpp (overlaps up to 1 MiB against a shadow buffer) do check correctness.

The cited CSV does not record its build. The 'libc' label holds only for duck's hosted default; in a freestanding -k build, cmemory/memcpy.hpp defines extern "C" memcpy on top of micron's own __memcpy_bytes, so ::memcpy would no longer be glibc.

mc::memcpy and mc::memmove convert element by element with static_cast when sizeof(F) != sizeof(D) or a type is not trivially copyable, so they do not always copy bytes; their count is in elements of the source type, while mc::memset counts bytes.
verified_claims_summary: On an Intel i7-5960X (Haswell-E, 20 MiB L3; CPU and the GCC 16.2.1 -O3 -march=native build are named only in sibling result files), with CPU 0 pinned and median of 5 batches of 16384 SPEC2017-distributed random copies, micron used 0.2803 vs 0.3480 cycles/byte for memcpy at 32 KiB and 0.3045 vs 0.4829 at 1 MiB (1.24x and 1.59x), 0.2377 vs 0.4532 for zero memset at 1 MiB (1.91x) and 0.3236 vs 0.4231 for memmove at 1 MiB (1.31x) against glibc of unstated version (ratios derived from page data). The same author's fixed-size detail runs show glibc faster overall for hot memcpy (geomean 0.96) and memmove (0.89) and for every cold memcpy cell.
status_note: Very active (last commit 2026-10-03, 407 commits) but a 13-star single-author project with no issue tracker activity and an explicitly unstable ABI; BSL-1.0 (abcmalloc MIT), so the cmemory headers can be vendored with their small simd/types dependencies.
